before.label: Geography & environmental inquiry
before.date_label: Nineteenth-century roots; regional, cultural and ecological inquiry
before.description: Several traditions ask how human activity and physical environments shape landscapes. Vidal investigates regional individuality; Marsh examines human environmental modification; Sauer relates physical and cultural forms; Leopold joins ecological observation with ethical concern. Their later uses differ, including Annales geography and environmental historians’ landscape inquiry. Critical and feminist geography add questions about capital, mobility, gender and contested place histories; Hayden and the History Workshop journal show specific historical uses. Driver examines the practices and disagreements of imperial geographical inquiry.

before.scope_note: Vidal’s human geography and Marsh’s environmental inquiry are different resources; neither defines all later environmental history. This is a selective set of resources for historians, not a complete history of geography. Sauer and Leopold supply distinct approaches; national framing, ecological care and landscape morphology are not a single programme. Harvey and Massey disagree within critical inquiry; neither stands for the whole discipline. Colonial frameworks are investigated as historically situated practices with internal conflicts. This expanded selection still does not represent global geography comprehensively.

before.label: Environmental history
before.description: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature. These approaches disagree about causal emphasis. Cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecological processes with power without supplying one universal model.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977. Expanded contextual readings include Leopold’s precursor essays, Melville’s Mexican study, Gadgil and Guha’s Indian history, Grove’s colonial conservation and Carruthers’s South African park history.

representative_people.context: Argues that organisms accompanying Europeans helped transform environments and sustain settler expansion, particularly in temperate regions.
representative_people.works: Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986)

representative_people.context: Connects the Dust Bowl with agricultural capitalism as well as environmental conditions; this is a contested explanation, not the field’s unanimous account.
representative_people.works: Dust Bowl: The Southern Plains in the 1930s (1979); “The Dirty Thirties: A Study in Agricultural Capitalism” (1986)

representative_people.context: Brings feminist history of science into environmental inquiry; argues that mechanical conceptions of nature support new forms of control and capitalist development.
representative_people.works: The Death of Nature: Women, Ecology, and the Scientific Revolution (1980)

representative_people.context: Links colonial property and ecological change, city–hinterland commodity flows, and cultural ideas of wilderness. His later afterword criticizes schematic capitalism and uneven treatment of Indigenous and colonial sources in his first book.
representative_people.works: Changes in the Land (1983); Nature’s Metropolis (1991); “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995)

representative_people.context: Ecological observation and conservation ethics precede the field’s later consolidation; Cronon identifies a landscape-training model drawn from Leopold.

representative_people.context: Ecologist collaborating with Ramachandra Guha on resource-use systems and their social and political conflicts in India.
representative_people.works: With Ramachandra Guha, This Fissured Land: An Ecological History of India (1992; UC Press edition 1993)

representative_people.context: Traces conservation ideas through colonial island settings and scientific networks; his geographical emphasis differs from histories of mainland African conservation.
representative_people.works: Green Imperialism: Colonial Expansion, Tropical Island Edens and the Origins of Environmentalism, 1600–1860 (1995)

representative_people.context: Examines South African conservation through the politics of Kruger National Park, racial power and Afrikaner nationalism.
representative_people.works: The Kruger National Park: A Social and Political History (1995)

representative_people.context: Adapts Crosby’s biological-conquest question to introduced grazing animals and social change in Mexico’s Valle del Mezquital, emphasizing places with continuing Indigenous populations.
representative_people.works: A Plague of Sheep: Environmental Consequences of the Conquest of Mexico (1994)

before.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship.

strands.title: Organisms, conquest and ecological exchange

strands.works: Ecological Imperialism (1986); A Plague of Sheep (1994)

strands.title: Agricultural capitalism and environmental crisis
strands.focus: Worster connects the Dust Bowl to agricultural capitalism. Compare that argument with competing explanations instead of treating it as settled consensus.

strands.title: Gender, science and the control of nature
strands.focus: Merchant’s feminist intervention joins history of science with environmental questions; her mechanical-order argument concerns ideas, power and material change.

strands.title: Colonial property and ecological change
strands.focus: Property concepts help Cronon explain changes in New England. Read with his later self-criticism about source asymmetry, spirituality and schematic capitalism.
strands.works: Changes in the Land (1983; retrospective afterword 2003)

strands.title: Cities, commodities and hinterlands
strands.focus: Follow lumber, grain and meat between rural production and urban processing and markets; follow capital back toward the countryside.
strands.works: Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991)

strands.title: Resource use and social conflict in India
strands.focus: Changing resource-use systems, state interventions and resistance connect ecological and social histories without making precolonial society uniformly harmonious.

strands.title: Conservation, colonial science and racial power
strands.focus: Grove studies colonial conservation networks and islands; Carruthers studies a South African park’s racial and national politics. These distinct scales complicate a purely benevolent conservation story.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Wilderness as a historical cultural idea
strands.focus: Cronon examines the pristine-wilderness ideal and Indigenous removal, while defending care for nonhuman nature in inhabited places.

added.evidence_note: Morphology reprint 347–348 directly discusses La Terre and Berr’s foreword. Sauer values their attack on environmentalist explanations but calls their knowledge of geographical thought limited and questions their elevation of Vidal. This is Sauer’s specific judgment, not a verdict shared by all geographers.

verification.note: UQAM transcription of the 1949 Albin Michel edition: complete 1922 and 1924 avertissements, PDF 25–27; selected introduction PDF 47–51; selected Part I chapter I PDF 90–97 and opening of 98 read. PDF pagination is reflowed, not original print pagination. Febvre directly discusses Vidal’s regional method and quotes his refusal both to explain history wholly by geography and to dispense with geography. He distinguishes human landscape modification from environmental determination and asks for historical evidence and multiple causes. His portrayal of Ratzel and national traditions remains attributed, not a uniform French/German opposition. The 1922 notice credits Bataillon’s notes and suggestions for specified parts; this is acknowledged collaboration, not sole or equal authorship. Original 1922 metadata independently checked at https://bibdig.biblioteca.unesp.br/items/f4e9fbce-f0ad-4ecc-8082-793e40e312bc . Full book, original printing and the cited Vidal articles not collated; Berr’s separate avant-propos not read.

added.citation: Lucien Febvre, Combats pour l’histoire (1953; consulted 1992 edition), selected preface and “Deux amis géographes: Jules Sion, Albert Demangeon.”

verification.note: Read preface PDF 12 and complete opening/section I on Sion, PDF 432–437 (printed 375–380), plus section II opening PDF 437–438 (printed 380–381). At printed 378 Febvre recalls proposing Sion for Berr’s geographical book; Sion, committed to Vidal’s Asian volumes, instead enlisted Vidal to encourage Febvre. This is retrospective author testimony about encouragement and collaboration, not proof of formal supervision. The collection date is 1953; original essay date not independently established here. The Demangeon section and full collection remain unread. Sion’s Asian geographical portraits are described as Febvre’s assessments, not independently verified field knowledge. Separate source febvre_combats_primary retains the earlier reading scope.

verification.note: Primary article PDF: abstract and opening 45–47, section Landscape and the Humanist Tradition in Geography 56–59, acknowledgments and relevant notes 65–79 read. Full intervening Renaissance case analysis and images not examined. Explicitly cites Sauer’s Morphology and contests claims of a neutral areal concept; argues that visual conventions and property relations require historical criticism. His claim that chorological results lack process is retained as criticism, not substituted for Sauer’s explicit account of changing landscapes. Note 68 prints Sauer’s date as 1926; Sauer’s own scanned reprint identifies 1925, which the graph retains. Does not certify all European visual history or every geographical use of landscape.

verification.note: Six-page primary syllabus read through indexed PDF text. Page 4 assigns Sauer’s “Foreword to Historical Geography” (1941), Land and Life 351–379, in the 14 September session, alongside other landscape and environmental-history readings. This establishes a named pre-2001 teaching use, not a claim that the class assigned Morphology (1925), that all students adopted Sauer, or that Sauer alone founded environmental history. verification.note: Expanded check: all 19 public scan images of the Land and Life reprint, printed 315–350, read through image inspection and local OCR, including notes. Opening four scan pages (printed 315–321) visually compared with the unfinished transcription; substantive opening claims confirmed, without claiming a perfect diplomatic transcription. Cultural-landscape diagram and surrounding text 342–343 and Febvre criticism 348–349 visually checked. Remaining pages read in OCR; no complete image-by-image textual collation. Reprint footnote identifies original 1925 publication 19–54; original printing not independently collated. Handwritten cover mentions 1983 [1963], not independently verified reprint metadata. Sauer distinguishes landscape morphology from geomorphology, proposes reconstructing past cultural landscapes, attributes agency to culture, cites Vidal, and both praises and criticizes Febvre/Berr at 347–348. His value-free claim, culture-cycle vocabulary and disciplinary portraits remain attributed. Final scan also contains opening of the next 1941 essay, not its full text. Later reception separately documented by Cosgrove 1985 and Cronon 1994 sources. First scan: https://www.fromthepage.com/kgeographer/cultural-landscape/sauer-morphology/display/32031536 ; final scan: display/32031554.

outcomes.finding: The opening Sauer transcription is checked against its scan and the full reprinted essay read through images/OCR. Historical reconstruction is distinguished from claims of neutral morphology; Cosgrove supplies explicit later criticism. Cronon’s 1994 syllabus supplies a specific teaching use of Sauer’s separate 1941 essay. Febvre’s own book directly uses Vidal, while his memoir identifies Sion/Vidal encouragement and his author notice credits Bataillon. Sauer both uses and criticizes Febvre/Berr, now represented by distinct directed exchanges.
outcomes.research_limit: Original Sauer 1925 printing not collated; 19-image Land and Life reprint read, opening four images visually compared and selected later images inspected, remaining pages read in OCR. No complete diplomatic collation. Cosgrove selected opening/concluding sections and relevant notes, not full Renaissance case analysis/images. Cronon syllabus demonstrates assignment, not assent; full Sauer 1941 essay unread. Febvre selected passages in later editions only, not full books or original Vidal sources. Memoir encouragement is retrospective testimony; original essay date not established. This is a bounded reception sample, not exhaustive reception history.
